Header: Septoria lactucae Lettuce leaf spot and blight, Septoria spot, Septoria leaf spot

Prevention: Use certified, disease free seeds for planting
Avoid high density seedings on nursery beds to improve aeration
Select healthy plants from nursery for transplanting, remove any seedlings showing symptoms
Avoid using the same location for the nursery year after year to prevent build up of the fungus
Control weeds, volunteer crops and wild lettuce crops since these plants can host the fungus
Avoid overhead irrigation since the disease develops in wet conditions and spreads via splashing.
Irrigate in the morning to minimize periods of leaf wetness
Mulch with straw or other available materials after transplanting to reduce rain splash
Avoid working in fields when plants are wet to prevent disease spread
Disinfect farm implements/tools with fire or household bleach (1 part bleach to 1 part water) to avoid spreading the disease
Rotate with non-host crops for 3 years such as maize, millet, sorghum, cowpea and cassava
After harvest, plough crop debris into the soil to speed up decomposition.
Crop debris can otherwise host the fungus
Monitoring: Symptoms start on the oldest leaves, consisting of small, irregular yellow spots
Lesions become larger, turn brown, dry and may fall out, making the leaves look tattered
Old lesions turn necrotic and become sunken
The lower leaves progressively die and drop off
The leaf spots contain brown/black dots which are fungal reproductive structures (pycnidia)
In severe cases symptoms occur on stems and petioles of the plant as well
Consider applying direct control immediately when the first spots are observed
Direct Control: If the disease density is low
rogue out infected plants immediately when they are observed and destroy by deeply burying (at least 1 m deep) or burning
